answer: DeepWalk generalizes neural language models by treating node sequences generated by random walks on a graph as if they were sentences of text. Each node plays the role of a word, and each random walk plays the role of a sentence or document. DeepWalk runs truncated random walks from the graph's nodes to produce these 'sentences,' then applies a Skip-gram-style language model (word2vec-like, trained with hierarchical softmax or negative sampling) to learn representations that maximize the likelihood of nodes appearing within a window of context nodes. Because the random walks capture local neighborhood structure, nodes that co-occur in walks (i.e., are close in the graph) end up with similar embeddings. Given a graph as input, DeepWalk therefore outputs a low-dimensional, continuous vector representation (embedding) for each node, typically a matrix with one row per node and a fixed number of latent dimensions, which can be used for tasks such as node classification, link prediction, and visualization.
